title: Famed Tom & Jerry Christmas House Demolished to Make Way For Two-Unit Building
summary: Just as the holiday season kicks into high gear, we have news that a longtime seasonal touchstone and spectacle near the Castro neighborhood has been torn down.
content: Just as the holiday season kicks into high gear, we have news that a longtime seasonal touchstone and spectacle near the Castro neighborhood has been torn down. The famous Tom & Jerry Christmas House at 3650 21st Street is no more, three years after the death of owner Dr. Jerome "Jerry" Goldstein . Goldstein's partner of 48 years, Tom Taylor, passed away in 2020. As the Chronicle reports , the modest three-story Victorian on the steep hill of 21st near Church Street, in Dolores Heights, has been demolished. Last year, plans were filed for a new, three-story, two-unit building — and the renderings, for what they're worth, appear to show that the famous live fir tree on the property that annually got festooned with thousands of lights will be preserved under the plans. Mission Local noted earlier this year that the home could have been a candidate for historic preservation, though a demolition permit was quickly issued. It's not clear if anyone undertook a preservation effort for the property at all, and pressures to build more housing — in this case one extra unit — have been impacting preservation decisions more broadly. The Tom & Jerry House hasn't seen its excessive holiday decorations for the past six years — the last time was in 2020, in commemoration of Taylor's passing that fall. Taylor, a longtime event and retail display designer, took on the Christmas decorating project just for fun, decorating their Norfolk Island pine tree in the front yard. The tree, as the story goes, began as a three-foot-tall houseplant that outgrew their living room around 1973, so they planted it outside. As Taylor told SFist back in 2015, "Then it got really big and the roots found the sewer pipe and went crazy." The tree ultimately grew to over 65 feet, and by the 2010s, Taylor was no longer stringing lights or hanging the outsized ornaments himself — it required a special crew the couple brought in each year. "It has all types of ornaments on it, it’s not like Macy’s with all one type," Taylor said. "I don’t do ‘theme’ things, that’s for the department stores. The scale just got bigger as the tree got bigger." From the tree, the display expanded to the front of the house itself and the area around the tree, which would feature a small Ferris wheel, a model train, various stuffed animals and oversized wrapped presents, and two giant stockings hanging over the garage with the names Tom and Jerry on them. San Francisco restaurateur and onetime Amazing Race winner Tyler MacNiven gave a little tour of the display in 2010 for SF Secrets that you can see below. Taylor was also known for being the "Keeper of the Rainbow Flag," maintaining and replacing the giant rainbow flag in Harvey Milk Plaza whenever necessary. And Goldstein worked for decades as a gay rights activist, in addition to his work a neurologist who specialized in headaches. Both were friends with rainbow flag co-creator Gilbert Baker, who served as an officiant at their 2013 wedding ceremony. The Tom & Jerry House was featured on The Great Christmas Light Fight in 2018, but Taylor was most proud of the documentary short that was made about the house, titled Making Christmas: The View from the Tom & Jerry Christmas Tree , which screened at Frameline in 2011. After that, DVD copies of the film were for sale each year at the house's concession stand. As Goldstein told SFist, the annual display was part of the work the couple always strove to do, to help people and bring joy to the community, through philanthropy. "Some people like to write checks. We like to do good deeds," he said. RIP, Tom, Jerry, and the Tom & Jerry House.
